The point I am more interested in is what people think, aside from the whole childishness of the littering ticket for spilled champagne and whatnot, of the point raised about corporate sponsorship being involved in something like the AT.

In the other thread we briefly discussed how little of a margin he beat the record by - basically a few hours. It worked out to him being like 0.27% faster or something (on mobile can't easily check).

What do people think about the level of assistance he got compared to the woman who held the previous record (who also had assistance, but not as extensive of a support team)? Scott is a professional runner in the sense that he gets paid to wear or endorse products like most of the top runners. So it isn't surprising that he would wear a Cliff Bar head band or have Brooks lettered on his support van. So now Cliff Bar and Brooks will have a commercial or two and some ads in some magazines about how their product helped Scott to set a new record on the AT. That isn't a bad thing in my opinion. I think it is safe to say that almost anyone setting out to do what he did would seek endorsement deals and as much support as possible. I know I would have.

As far as for the level of support assisting him in beating the record by a few hours it may have helped some but on a journey that long and over that many days there are a lot of other variables that comes in to play. Injuries and bad weather for example. What were the trail conditions, dry or muddy? I think on runs such as this, each effort should be judged individually. I think that Scott would be the first one to concede that what he did takes absolutely nothing from efforts of past record holders like Jennifer Davis and David Horton. I'm gonna do this a bit quick. So, pushups. Everybody loves them. It's a good bodyweight chest thing. I have just some questions. Questions are in bold.

First of all, incline/decline pushups. Does the incline pushup target the lower chest and does the decline pushup target the upper chest? If I do incline pushups for 4 sets consisting of 10 repetitions for six months, will I get a overdeveloped lower chest with an underdeveloped upper chest? And vice-versa.

Second, how effective it is. Just how effective is the pushup for chest development? If I do some standard pushups for 4 sets consisting of 10 repetitions for six months, will I get the same development if I had done standard bench presses with the same weight for 4 sets consisting of 10 repetitions for six months instead?

Thanks for replying.

EDIT: Yes I know the weights being resisted are different, but let's assume every exercise mentioned deals the same resistance to the muscles involve.

Sorry for the late reply. There's not going to be a noticeable difference in your different parts of your chest based on that type of exercise, since mostly it only changes range of motion. The push-up can be an effective tool for chest development, but it is much easier to gain mass with weights. Gaining mass with bodyweight exercises is much trickier, and you won't be able to do it with standard push-ups. If you're adding weight to them remember-no once can do a push-up with more weight than a bench press. I can press 225 despite hardly ever having to prove it, but if you put that much weight on my back while I was doing push-ups, I'd die. But the push-up is much better for you than the bench (and if you do decide to go with weights, for the love of god, include the overhead press and chin-ups in your routine!) since it works more muscles without creating an imbalance, so if you can increase resistance linearly like with a bench, it will work the same muscle groups and more, provided you are actually using your chest muscles. It's entirely possible to do both of these exercises in such a way you will miss out almost entirely on chest development.

This is what the gifs I make, using ffmpeg, gimp, openshot/kdenlive, look like: gif1, gif2, gif3 9mb beware

The way I've been making gifs is to record the screen or a part of the screen: OBS, SimpleScreenRecorder, or an ffmepg script - here's mine: 

TIMESTAMP=$(date "+%Y-%m-%d %H:%M") 
~/bin/ffmpeg\
 -f alsa -thread_queue_size 2048 -i pulse -f x11grab -r 30 \
 -video_size 860x500 \
 -s 860x500 -thread_queue_size 512 -i :0.0+257,129 \
 -acodec libmp3lame -vcodec libx264 -preset ultrafast\
 -qp 0 -threads 0 \
 -f mp4 ~/"Videos/ffmpeg-`echo $TIMESTAMP`.mp4"

You can use something like Openshot or Kdenlive to cut out the portion of the video you want.

I've been using another ffmpeg script to turn those videos to individual pngs with this:

ffmpeg -i *.mp4 -r 30 ./frames/outputimages%04d.png
// or to cut out a 15 second segment. For video you could probably drop the 30 to 10, maybe
ffmpeg -i *.mp4 -ss 00:15:40 -t 00:00:15 -r 30 ./frames/outputimages%04d.png

I open the first image into GIMP, then open the rest of the images as layers. Doing this in gimp allows for easy cropping/resizing. Then I go to Filters -> Animation -> Optimize for Gif. Export it as a gif and set the delay of all frames to 33ms, since I capture at 30 frames per second.

I think the jittery artifacts you sometimes see is because I'm making them on my laptop with open source radeon drivers. The transparent blue floor tiles in gif 1 and 2 are due to having the collision layer visible and transparent.

Edit: forgot to add kdenlive and openshot for video editing.
